why: A glossary nobody can check is a document. Every term here names the one artifact in the tree that owns it, so two words that mean the same thing cannot both be canonical and a word that quietly acquired a second meaning fails rather than drifts.

terms.means: the person who signed in; the thing a login resolves to and the thing a row belongs to
the scope a row is filed under, which is a question about the row and never an object in its own right
the billed and governed company an account belongs to; the object a tenant scope points at
the named container a member switches between, personal or organizational; it is not the organization, because a personal one has no organization at all
something the product can do on a surface, before anybody asks whether this caller may
what the plan the account pays for carries
what the organization has decided its members may do, whatever their plan carries
what this member's role lets them administer, whatever the organization allows its members generally
the stored thread of messages; chat is the surface it is read on
a document or program the assistant produced that the user keeps
a connection to a third party the account authorized
a task the product runs later without being asked again

distinctions.why: conflating them is how a personal workspace inherits an organization's policy and how deleting a company deletes a person
each answers a different question, so a refusal that names the wrong one sends the user to buy an upgrade that cannot help them

conflations.why: one concept owns the table for the container and the table for the company, so nothing in the registry distinguishes a personal workspace from the organization a workspace may belong to, and workspaces.kind is the only thing that does
conflations.fix: split the registry entry into an organization concept over organizations and organization_members and a workspace concept over workspaces, with the workspace parented on the organization when workspaces.kind is organization
